title: Science in the Lab
short: CT scans look inside mummies without unwrapping them; studies of ancient DNA, residues and isotopes are newer and still debated in places.
trouble: Students take every science headline as settled. New methods need careful checking, and results are often revised.

blocks.html: Some of the newest evidence about ancient Egypt comes from laboratories, not trenches. Survey sees under the ground; lab science sees inside objects and bodies, often without harming them.

CT scanning looks inside mummies without unwrapping them, showing age, health, injuries and how the body was prepared. Ancient DNA, residue analysis (what was in a pot) and isotope studies (what people ate and where they grew up) are newer; their results are exciting but often small in scale and still debated.

A new method is only as good as its checks. CT scans are images that many doctors can read and compare, so their basic results are rarely in doubt. Ancient DNA, by contrast, is fragile and easily contaminated by modern DNA, and a study may rest on a few individuals from one site. A careful reader asks: how many samples, from where, and has another team confirmed it?

blocks.name: eg-pyramid
blocks.cap: The Great Pyramid's known passages and chambers. In 2017 muon imaging found a large void above the Grand Gallery, and in 2023 a corridor behind the north face was confirmed with a camera on a probe. What the void was for is still unknown.

blocks.title: Reading a headline
blocks.q: A headline says: "DNA reveals the true origins of the ancient Egyptians." What should you ask before believing it?
steps: How many individuals were tested, and from which sites and periods? One cemetery cannot speak for all of Egypt over three thousand years.
Were contamination checks reported, and has another lab confirmed the result?
What do other scholars say? The 2017 Abusir el-Meleq study, for example, has been praised as a technical first and criticized for its small sample from one site.
blocks.a: Ask about sample size, checks and confirmation.

blocks.title: What a scan can show
blocks.q: Why is a CT scan of a mummy better than unwrapping it, as was often done in the 1800s?
steps: Unwrapping destroys the wrappings and often damages the body.
A scan shows bones, teeth, packing, amulets and embalming work in three dimensions, with no harm.
The scan can be shared and re-examined as questions change.
blocks.a: It shows the inside without destroying anything.

blocks.html: Taking every science headline as settled. New methods need careful checking, and results are often revised. Look for the sample size, whether others have confirmed it, and whether the article says what is still debated.
